title: Adaptive Residual Learning for Robust Visual Recognition
authors: Alice Chen; Bob Wang; Carol Li
abstract: Deeper visual recognition networks are difficult to train and existing architectures show insufficient feature selection capability in complex scenes. To address this challenge, we propose an adaptive residual learning framework with a self-gating mechanism that dynamically recalibrates feature responses across channels. Our method, termed ARL-Net, achieves a top-5 error rate of 5.2% on a large-scale benchmark, outperforming standard residual baselines by 1.8% on average across multiple visual tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate stable convergence and improved robustness under noisy labels.

title: Multi-Scale Feature Aggregation for Efficient Object Detection
authors: Dave Zhang; Eve Liu; Frank Zhao
abstract: Object detection at multiple scales remains a core challenge, and existing approaches cannot effectively handle extreme scale variations across objects. The bottleneck lies in the inability of single-scale features to capture multi-scale context efficiently. We introduce a multi-scale feature aggregation network combined with a class-balanced loss that mitigates foreground-background imbalance during training. Our method achieves 39.4 mAP on a public detection benchmark, improving over strong baselines by 2.6 mAP while reducing inference latency by 25%.

title: Global-Local Attention Networks for Image Classification
authors: Grace Sun; Henry Xu; Ivy Wu
abstract: While convolutional networks dominate image classification, capturing long-range dependencies between image regions remains an open problem, and stacking deep layers for global context is computationally inefficient. We propose a global-local attention network (GLANet) that alternately applies patch-level self-attention and spatial convolution in a single unified architecture. Pre-trained on large unlabeled image collections and fine-tuned on standard benchmarks, GLANet reaches 87.1% top-1 accuracy on a large-scale visual benchmark, outperforming convolution-only counterparts with 30% fewer FLOPs.

title: Progressive Noise Removal for High-Fidelity Image Synthesis
authors: Jack Ma; Kevin Zhou; Lily Tang
abstract: Generative image modeling faces the persistent challenge of balancing sample quality with diversity, and adversarial training often suffers from mode collapse while autoregressive models are slow at high resolutions. We present a progressive denoising pipeline with classifier-free guidance that first generates a low-resolution image and then refines it through a sequence of super-resolution progressive refinement stages. Our method achieves an generation quality score of 6.8 on a 256x256 generation benchmark, surpassing strong GAN baselines while reducing total sampling cost by 35%.

title: Prompt-Guided Universal Segmentation Framework
authors: Mona Feng; Nick Guo; Oliver Yang
abstract: Image segmentation systems are typically designed for specific tasks and generalize poorly across diverse segmentation scenarios, limiting their application to real-world problems. We introduce a prompt-guided universal segmentation framework that accepts point, box, and sketch prompts through a shared prompt encoder. Trained on a large curated dataset of 8M images with 800M mask annotations, the model segments arbitrary objects with zero-shot transfer, reaching 93% of fully supervised specialists' performance on 18 benchmark datasets without fine-tuning.

title: Lightweight Cross-Modal Fusion with Shared Semantic Space
authors: Penny Xie; Quincy Luo; Rachel He
abstract: Multi-modal learning systems often suffer from high computational cost and difficulty aligning representations across modalities, and existing methods cannot transfer knowledge between modalities without expensive paired data. We design a lightweight cross-modal fusion module with a shared semantic embedding space, combined with a distillation schedule that transfers knowledge from a strong visual teacher to a compact multi-modal student. The approach reduces model size by 55% while improving multi-modal classification accuracy by 3.2% on image-text benchmarks, and remains robust with only 30% of labeled paired samples.

title: Temporal-Aware Implicit Neural Rendering for Dynamic Scenes
authors: Sam Lin; Tina Cao; Uma Shen
abstract: Implicit neural representations have shown impressive results in novel view synthesis, but applying them to dynamic scenes on resource-constrained devices remains an unresolved challenge due to the heavy computational cost of per-frame volumetric rendering. We present TINeRF, a temporal-aware implicit rendering variant that employs dynamic hash encoding and temporal feature caching. Our method achieves real-time 28 FPS rendering of dynamic scenes on mobile GPUs, a 45x speedup over vanilla implicit rendering, with PSNR of 30.4 dB on dynamic scene benchmarks comparable to desktop-class methods.

title: Bidirectional Context Encoding for Deep Language Understanding
authors: Victor Gao; Wendy Fang; Xavier Kong
abstract: Language model pre-training has shown great promise, but existing approaches are limited by unidirectional context, which restricts the representational power of pre-trained representations for downstream understanding tasks. We introduce a bidirectional context encoder that jointly conditions on both left and right context in all layers through masked language modeling. Our model obtains state-of-the-art results on nine natural language understanding benchmarks, pushing the aggregate multi-task score to 78.3% (an absolute improvement of 6.5%) and eliminating the need for heavily engineered task-specific architectures.

title: Unsupervised Multi-Task Learning via Scalable Autoregressive Pre-training
authors: Yuki Ito; Zach Pan; Aaron Qiu
abstract: Natural language processing tasks typically require task-specific datasets and architectures, creating the challenge of building systems that generalize across diverse language tasks without explicit supervision. We demonstrate that autoregressive models trained on sufficiently large and diverse text corpora learn multiple NLP skills without supervised signals. Our model, a 1.2B-parameter autoregressive transformer trained on 6M web documents, achieves strong zero-shot results on 6 of 8 tested language benchmarks, including 52.1% accuracy on a conversational question-answering task without any task-specific training.

title: Knowledge-Enhanced Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
authors: Bella Han; Chris Ren; Diana Mao
abstract: Large pre-trained language models store factual knowledge implicitly, but they face the challenge of accessing and updating knowledge precisely without retraining. We propose a knowledge-enhanced retrieval generation framework that combines parametric memory with a differentiable retriever over an external knowledge corpus. Our approach achieves an exact-match score of 41.3 on an open-domain QA benchmark and 36.8 on a trivia benchmark, and generates more specific and factual responses, with an 11% improvement in factual consistency on knowledge-intensive tasks.

title: Efficient Model Adaptation with Sparse Low-Rank Updates
authors: Eric Jiang; Fiona Tao; Gary Xu
abstract: Adapting large pre-trained language models to downstream tasks is computationally prohibitive for most practitioners because it requires updating billions of parameters. The fundamental challenge is how to adapt models efficiently without sacrificing performance. We propose a sparse low-rank update method that freezes the pre-trained weights and injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices into attention layers. Our method reduces trainable parameters by 8000x compared to full fine-tuning on a 175B-scale model, maintains or exceeds full fine-tuning quality with 90.2% average score on a a multi-task language benchmark, and cuts GPU memory requirements by 3x.

title: Self-Consistent Stepwise Reasoning for Complex Mathematical Problems
authors: Helen Lei; Ivan Shen; Julia Kong
abstract: Large language models struggle with complex multi-step reasoning tasks because direct answer prediction often fails on problems requiring intermediate logical steps, hindering their application to mathematical reasoning. We explore stepwise reasoning prompts that generate explicit intermediate chains, combined with a self-consistency decoding strategy that samples multiple chains and selects the majority answer. On a grade-school math benchmark, our approach with a 540B-scale model achieves 55.4% accuracy, surpassing strong fine-tuned baselines by 21 points, and self-consistency decoding further improves results to 72.8%.

title: Language-Aware Expert Routing for Multilingual Neural Translation
authors: Kyle Meng; Laura Zhou; Max Zheng
abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation faces the challenge of negative interference between languages, where adding more languages to a single model degrades quality for low-resource languages. The core issue is that model capacity is shared across all language pairs without proper isolation. We adopt a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture with language-aware routing, designing dedicated expert modules that activate selectively per language pair. Our model achieves a 41% BLEU improvement for low-resource languages while maintaining quality for high-resource pairs, supporting 180 languages in a single model with an average gain of 4.8 BLEU points.

title: Progressive Reasoning Distillation for Compact Language Models
authors: Nina Wu; Oliver Bai; Paul Ren
abstract: The trend of scaling language models to hundreds of billions of parameters raises the problem of prohibitive deployment costs, and small models typically lack the reasoning capabilities of their larger counterparts. We employ a progressive reasoning distillation pipeline that transfers reasoning skills from large teacher models to compact student models through curated step-by-step traces. Our distilled 7B-scale model retains 86% of the teacher's reasoning performance while being 10x smaller and 14x more energy-efficient at inference, improving small-model accuracy from 44.8% to 60.2% on a multi-task reasoning benchmark.

title: Graph-Structured Message Passing for Molecular Property Prediction
authors: Quinn Shi; Rita Zhao; Steve Hu
abstract: Predicting molecular properties from graph-structured data is crucial for drug discovery, yet existing methods struggle to capture both local chemical substructures and long-range molecular interactions simultaneously, and traditional fingerprint approaches lack the flexibility to learn task-specific representations. We introduce a graph message passing framework that learns molecular representations directly from structures through iterative message exchange between atoms. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on 11 of 15 quantum property benchmarks, reducing mean absolute error by 20% compared to fingerprint methods and generalizing well to unseen molecules.

title: Novelty-Seeking Agents for Navigation in Unseen Environments
authors: Tom Wei; Vera Qiao; Will Shi
abstract: Autonomous navigation in unseen environments remains difficult for reinforcement learning agents due to sparse reward signals and the inability to explore efficiently in large state spaces, where standard strategies such as epsilon-greedy are insufficient for complex 3D tasks. We design a novelty-driven exploration module that rewards agents for discovering novel states, combined with a hierarchical control framework. Our approach enables agents to navigate complex unseen environments with a 96% success rate, improving over baseline exploration strategies by 32%, and learns to map a multi-room layout within 12M training steps.

title: Differentiable Constraint Learning for Scalable Causal Discovery
authors: Xin Luo; Yuki Pan; Zoe Li
abstract: Discovering causal relationships from purely observational data is a fundamental challenge in machine learning, and existing constraint-based and score-based methods suffer from searching over the combinatorial space of directed acyclic graphs, which grows super-exponentially with the number of variables. We formulate structure learning as a continuous optimization problem with a differentiable acyclicity constraint, enabling gradient-based search. Our method reduces computation time from hours to minutes on graphs with 50+ nodes while achieving 12-25% better structural accuracy than combinatorial search baselines.

title: Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Learning with Efficient Gradient Aggregation
authors: Andy Sun; Beth Ma; Carl Xu
abstract: Collaborative learning enables model training across distributed clients without sharing raw data, but faces the dual challenges of preserving user privacy and reducing communication costs between clients and the central server, where standard averaging requires many rounds and may leak sensitive information. We present a federated averaging framework enhanced with formal privacy guarantees and a gradient compression scheme that reduces communication overhead by 82%. Our method achieves accuracy within 1.1% of centralized training while providing formal (epsilon=8, delta=1e-5) privacy guarantees and scales to 10,000+ clients with heterogeneous data.

title: Self-Supervised Contrastive Pretraining for Time-Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Dana Wu; Evan Lin; Fiona Zhao
abstract: Time-series anomaly detection is critical for industrial monitoring yet suffers from severe class imbalance, since anomalies are rare and diverse, making supervised approaches impractical and labeled anomaly samples unavailable at training time. We adopt a self-supervised contrastive pretraining framework that learns robust time-series representations by distinguishing original signals from carefully designed augmented segments. Our method achieves a 95.2% F1 score on an industrial control benchmark, improving over the previous best unsupervised method by 7.6%, and the learned representations transfer to new anomaly types without additional training.

title: Emergent Communication Protocols for Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination
authors: Gary Zhou; Helen Wu; Ivan Ma
abstract: Coordinating multiple AI agents in partially observable environments presents the challenge of learning cooperative behaviors without centralized control, and existing multi-agent learning methods often fail to scale beyond a handful of agents due to the combinatorial explosion of the joint action space. We propose an emergent communication framework in which agents learn a discrete signaling protocol alongside their policies, enabling coordinated planning across 40+ agents. Our framework achieves 91% task completion in cooperative navigation and resource allocation tasks, compared to 58% for independent learners, and the emergent protocol exhibits interpretable structure encoding spatial and priority information.
